title: Develop quality plans and ensure overall quality of products or services in a small business or business unit

lessons.title: Defining quality and developing a quality plan
lessons.html:
What quality means for a small business

Quality is meeting the customer's requirements consistently. For a small packhouse, a cold store, a contract harvesting team or a transport business, quality has two sides:

  • Product quality: the fruit, cartons or pallets meet the agreed specification.
  • Service quality: reliability, timeliness, communication and accuracy, for example delivering bins when promised or sending correct documents.

Poor quality has costs: rework, downgrades, claims, lost customers and wasted time. These are often called the cost of poor quality, and they are usually far higher than the cost of preventing problems.

Developing a quality plan

A quality plan sets out how a business or unit will make sure a product or service meets requirements. Steps:

  1. Identify customers and their requirements: specifications, standards (such as export standards under the APS Act), certification requirements and service expectations. Write them down.
  2. Map the process: list each step from receiving inputs to delivering the product or service.
  3. Identify what can go wrong at each step and how serious it would be.
  4. Set controls: what will be checked, how, how often, by whom and against what standard.
  5. Define records: which forms or systems will capture the checks.
  6. Plan for non-conformance: what to do when a check fails.
  7. Assign responsibilities and training.
  8. Set measurable objectives: for example inspection pass rate, on-time delivery, number of complaints.

Example quality plan extract

StepControlFrequencyResponsible
Fruit receivingCheck bin labels and fruit temperatureEvery loadReceiving clerk
GradingQC sample against class specificationEvery hour per lineQC controller
PalletisingCheck carton marking and pallet cardEvery palletPallet supervisor
Cold storeRecord air and pulp temperatureTwice per shiftCold store operator

lessons.title: Implementing, monitoring and improving quality
lessons.html:
Putting the plan into practice

  • Communicate the plan to everyone involved, explaining why each check matters.
  • Train staff in the standards and methods; use reference samples and photographs of defects.
  • Provide resources: calibrated instruments, good lighting at grading tables, forms or tablets.
  • Display specifications at the workstation.
  • Supervise: supervisors check that controls are done and recorded correctly.

Monitoring quality

Collect data from checks and summarise it regularly. Useful tools for a small business include:

  • Check sheets: simple tallies of defects by type and time.
  • Pareto charts: rank problems from most to least frequent. Often a few causes create most of the problems, so fix those first.
  • Run charts: plot a measure over time, such as daily pass rate, to see trends.
  • Customer feedback: complaints, arrival reports and regular conversations.

Dealing with problems

  1. Contain the problem: isolate affected product.
  2. Find the root cause using questions such as why did this happen, repeated until you reach a cause you can fix. A fishbone diagram helps consider people, methods, machines, materials, measurement and environment.
  3. Take corrective action and record it.
  4. Check that the action worked.
  5. Update the quality plan and training if needed.

Continuous improvement

Use the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. Involve workers, who often know best where problems come from. Hold short quality meetings at the start of shifts during the season. Recognise teams that achieve their targets.

Example

A small packhouse finds that most inspection failures are due to marking errors. A Pareto chart shows two causes: wrong count stamps and missing PUC codes. The owner introduces a check at the start of each packing run and a colour-coded stamp system. Failures from marking drop sharply within two weeks.

Key points

  • Quality is consistently meeting customer requirements for product and service.
  • A quality plan lists controls, frequency, responsibility and records for each step.
  • Train staff, provide resources and display specifications.
  • Use check sheets, Pareto charts and run charts to monitor quality.
  • Find root causes and use Plan-Do-Check-Act to improve.
